rationale:
Today's slate stays inside the plague focus and covers 5 different focus pillars: Lab safety (L1 and S1), The news, decoded (S2), Symptoms and urgent care (S3), and History versus now plus Myths (C1). Every pillar we were given is a GLP-1 playlist, and none of them fits plague, so every piece goes in "general" (Health Science Explained). The mix follows the brief. About half the slate is early or rising news: the lab-safety explainer and its spin-off are at the emerging stage with little competition, and the Oct 8 status update and the symptoms Short are at the peaking or rising stage. The Black Death vs 2026 carousel is the evergreen piece, and it also does the myth-correcting work, aimed at the "untreatable, medieval, could happen again" beliefs. Several topics are left out because we covered them in the last 30 days:
- the Oct 7 status decoder, which already explained how plague is confirmed in a lab, so I dropped the diagnosis long-form
- Madagascar 2017 and the exposure steps
- person-to-person spread, curability, US cases and travellers
- vaccines, risk levels and the 3-forms carousel

Symptoms and urgent care had not been covered yet, and the analytics playbook names it as a priority title. S1 is a spin-off of L1 so it sends viewers to the long video. The lab-safety and status-update pieces are marked caution on the radar, so both get the careful treatment:
- They use only attributed, dated facts ("suspected/reported", "as of Oct 8, 2026", credited to Rospotrebnadzor, WHO or CDC).
- They don't speculate about a leak or bioweapon, and they don't blame or name the worker.
- They don't repeat rumours.
- Every piece carries the line "If you're worried, talk to a health professional."

pieces.topic: How labs that study plague keep it contained: biosafety levels (BSL-3), airflow, PPE, and standard steps after a possible lab exposure
pieces.angle: Plague Labs: How Do Scientists Keep Dangerous Bacteria Contained? A general biosafety explainer from CDC/NIH BMBL (6th ed.) and WHO's Laboratory Biosafety Manual (4th ed.). What biosafety levels mean, and how BMBL scales Y. pestis work: BSL-2 practices and facilities for most clinical-sample and culture work, BSL-3 for aerosol-generating, large-scale or some animal work. Say clearly that this is the US/WHO framework and that countries, including Russia, use their own classification systems. Cover inward airflow and HEPA exhaust, biosafety cabinets, respirators and PPE, training and incident reporting. Then the standard post-exposure steps: report straight away, medical review, monitoring through the incubation window, and preventive antibiotics only when clinicians decide they're needed (no self-treatment). Dated status box: 'As of Oct 8, 2026: plague was suspected in media reports and has not been officially confirmed. Rospotrebnadzor reported that nearly 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens, that medical monitoring was completed for over 90% of contacts, and that quarantine measures were lifted in Irkutsk oblast. WHO says it does not know what caused the Oct 2 death and has asked Russia for more information. Not confirmed isn't ruled out.' Credit any incident detail to a named outlet ('reported by Reuters/AP'). No leak, bioweapon or blame framing, and don't name or show the worker. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Thumbnail: lab scene with a biosafety cabinet.
pieces.working_title: Plague Labs: How Do Scientists Keep Dangerous Bacteria Contained?
pieces.why: The radar puts this at the emerging stage (momentum 70, low competition, seen in 3 snapshots). NYT, Defector and The Conversation are covering the institute, but almost no explainer covers lab safety itself. It has 8–15 minutes of guideline-backed depth and is a pillar we haven't covered yet. | fact-check: Lab safety is a good, calm pillar, but two parts of the angle are wrong. (1) Scope: in the CDC/NIH BMBL agent summary for Yersinia pestis, BSL-2 practices, containment equipment and facilities are recommended for most work with clinical materials and cultures. BSL-3 is for work with a high potential for aerosol or droplet production, large-scale production, and some infected-animal work. So 'usually done at BSL-3' overstates it. (2) Status box: 'contact observation has ended' is stronger than the source. Rospotrebnadzor said medical monitoring was completed for 'over 90%' of contacts (reported Oct 8). The test figure was reported as 'nearly 5,000', not 'about 5,000'. The claim that 'no plague was recorded' came from Russian authorities via WHO, so credit it to them. Also: BSL-1 to BSL-4 is the US/WHO framework, and Russia classifies pathogens under its own system. Don't say or imply that the Irkutsk institute uses the BMBL BSL scheme. Leave out the governor's 'patient was vaccinated' claim, or credit it to him by name as a reported statement, with no inference. 'Lab-acquired plague is rare' needs a citable source (e.g. BMBL's note on reported laboratory-acquired infections). If you can't find one, drop it. Re-check the status at publish time.

pieces.topic: What does BSL-3 actually mean? The containment layers that keep plague inside a lab
pieces.angle: Plague Labs: What Does BSL-3 Actually Mean? One idea: BSL-3 is a set of containment layers. Air flows inward and is exhausted through HEPA filters, work happens inside biosafety cabinets, staff wear respirators and PPE, entry is controlled and incidents are reported straight away. Under CDC/NIH BMBL, plague work moves up to BSL-3 when it can create aerosols or involves large quantities, and most clinical-sample work uses BSL-2 practices. After a possible exposure: medical review, monitoring, and preventive antibiotics only if clinicians decide they're needed. Hedge line: 'Irkutsk oblast: plague suspected in media reports, not officially confirmed. WHO says the cause of death is not yet known (as of Oct 8, 2026).' Don't apply the BSL scheme to the Russian lab, and no leak speculation. Point to the full video. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Plague Labs: What Does BSL-3 Actually Mean?
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1, which drives traffic to the long video. It's an emerging question with low competition and a concrete subject plus a plain-question title. | fact-check: The same scope problem as L1. The working framing ('containment layers that keep plague inside a lab', with BSL-3 implied as the plague standard) misstates BMBL. BMBL recommends BSL-2 for most Y. pestis clinical and culture work, and BSL-3 for aerosol-prone or large-scale work. The hedge line is fine, but date it to the WHO statement (Oct 6–8) and say 'not officially confirmed'. Don't tie the BSL layers to the Irkutsk institute (Russia uses its own classification). Keep it to about 60 s and 170 words or fewer.

pieces.topic: Plague report in Russia, Oct 8 update: quarantine lifted and contact observation ended (Rospotrebnadzor), while WHO says the cause of death is still unconfirmed
pieces.angle: Plague Report in Russia: Quarantine Lifted. What's Confirmed? (as of Oct 8). Lines, each credited to its source: Rospotrebnadzor (Oct 8): nearly 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens, medical monitoring was completed for over 90% of contacts, quarantine measures were lifted, and it called reports of a second case 'fake'. WHO: it does not know what caused the Oct 2 death and has asked Russia for more information. WHO's initial risk assessment (reported Oct 6): moderate to low in Irkutsk oblast, low for Russia, very low for the WHO European Region. Teaching line: not confirmed isn't ruled out. Plague hasn't been officially confirmed. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' About 60–70 s.
pieces.working_title: Plague Report in Russia: Quarantine Lifted. What's Confirmed? (as of Oct 8)
pieces.why: The biggest status change since the death (radar momentum 93, peak in 0–3 days). The update angle is new, since the 10-07 decoder predates the lifted quarantine, and question-decoder titles are our proven format. | fact-check: A good dated decoder, but tighten three lines to match what was actually reported. (1) Rospotrebnadzor (Oct 8) reported medical monitoring completed for 'over 90%' of contacts, not 'contact observation has ended'. (2) The test figure was 'nearly 5,000'. (3) Rospotrebnadzor called the second-case reports 'fake' (AP/PBS, Oct 8); present that only as its denial. WHO's 'moderate to low / low / very low' rating is described as an initial risk assessment (reported Oct 6). PBS/AP reported that WHO had not issued a formal assessment, so call it 'WHO's initial risk assessment' and date it. WHO (Van Kerkhove, ~Oct 7–8) says it doesn't know what caused the Oct 2 death and has asked Russia for clarification. Re-check at publish time.

pieces.topic: Pneumonic plague symptoms and timing: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, typically 1–3 days after exposure (CDC), and when to get urgent care
pieces.angle: Pneumonic Plague Symptoms: When to Get Urgent Care (CDC). Within 10 s give CDC's list: fever, headache, weakness and a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and cough. Symptoms can start as soon as 1 day after breathing in the bacteria (CDC). Red flags only matter with a possible exposure: time in an area where plague occurs, contact with sick or dead animals or their fleas, or close contact with someone who has pneumonic plague. Action: contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and tell them about the exposure. No self-treatment or stockpiling. Calm payoff: plague is treatable with antibiotics, and CDC says prompt treatment is critical. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Pneumonic Plague Symptoms: When to Get Urgent Care (CDC)
pieces.why: It's a rising, high-demand search question (momentum 85) that we haven't covered yet, and the playbook names it directly as the next title to make in our best-reach format. | fact-check: A useful topic. CDC's public page lists 'fever, headache, weakness, and a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucus'. But the incubation wording the fact-checker could verify there is 'as short as 1 day' after inhalation, not 'typically 1–3 days'. Use CDC's wording exactly, or credit '1–3 days' to whichever source actually says it (e.g. the WHO fact sheet) after checking it. CDC's treatment line is 'Prompt treatment with the correct medications is critical to prevent complications or death.' Don't call antibiotics 'common', and don't say they 'work well', unless the cited CDC/WHO page says so. Tie the red flags to possible exposure.

pieces.topic: Black Death vs 2026: what germ theory, antibiotics and public health changed about plague
pieces.angle: Plague: Black Death vs 2026, What Actually Changed. Slide 1: 'Plague in the 1300s vs today: what germ theory, antibiotics and public health changed.' Slides 2–6, 1300s vs today: cause unknown vs Yersinia pestis identified (1894); fleas and rodents not understood vs known transmission routes (CDC); no effective treatment vs antibiotics, which work best when started early (CDC/WHO); no diagnosis vs lab testing; no tracing vs contact tracing, isolation and preventive antibiotics given by health authorities. Slide 7 myths: 'extinct': still occurs naturally, with an average of 7 human cases a year in the US (CDC, range 0–17). 'Untreatable': treatable with antibiotics, and prompt treatment is critical (CDC). Slide 8: red flags after possible exposure, plus 'contact a doctor or local health authority urgently'. Label death tolls as estimates, no doom words or graphic imagery, and close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
pieces.working_title: Plague: Black Death vs 2026, What Actually Changed
pieces.why: This is our evergreen and myth slot. It's a comparison that names both sides, has long-tail search value (RTE and Slate are revisiting the history), hasn't been covered yet, and works as a list people save. | fact-check: A good history-vs-now framework, and the facts check out: Yersin identified the bacterium in 1894, and CDC reports an average of 7 human cases a year (range 0–17). Problem: slide 1's hook 'Could the Black Death happen again?' is the doom framing the guardrails ban. Rewrite it as a calm comparison. In the 'no treatment' cell, say 'no effective treatment (antibiotics didn't exist)'. Label death tolls as estimates (e.g. 'estimated 30–50% of Europe's population'). On slide 7, write 'treatable, especially when antibiotics start early'. 'Contact tracing … and preventive antibiotics given by health authorities' must keep the authority wording.
